questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A tape unwinds with speed v from a roll rotating about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. The radius of the roll r is decreasing at a steady rate.

Which of the following graphs best represents the variation with time t of the speed v of the tape?
questions.stemText: A tape unwinds with speed v from a roll rotating about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. The radius of the roll r is decreasing at a steady rate. v r Which of the following graphs best represents the variation with time t of the speed v of the tape? A v 0 t B v 0 t C v t 0 D v 0 t

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must translate the steady decrease in radius into the shape of a speed–time graph.
questions.misconception: Equating constant angular velocity with constant linear speed

explanation.body: The tape speed is $v=r\omega$. With constant $\omega$ and a radius that decreases at a steady rate, the graph is a straight line with a negative gradient. The speed stays above zero while the radius is positive.

perOption.A: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant tape speed.
perOption.B: Shows the speed dropping more slowly over time, which would require the radius to shrink more slowly.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Shows the speed dropping faster over time, which would require the radius to shrink faster.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Three identical slotted masses are placed at 2R, 4R and 6R respectively from the centre of a horizontal rough disc of radius 10R.

The disc rotates about its centre O.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: Three identical slotted masses are placed at 2R, 4R and 6R respectively from the centre of a horizontal rough disc of radius 10R. The disc rotates about its centre O. Which statement is correct? A All three slotted masses experience the same centripetal force. B The slotted mass at 6R is most likely to move out of its circular path. C The slotted mass at 2R completes the least number of revolutions per unit time. D The slotted mass at 6R has three times the amount of kinetic energy as the slotted mass at 2R.

options.label: A
options.text: All three slotted masses experience the same centripetal force.

options.label: B
options.text: The slotted mass at 6R is most likely to move out of its circular path.

options.label: C
options.text: The slotted mass at 2R completes the least number of revolutions per unit time.

options.label: D
options.text: The slotted mass at 6R has three times the amount of kinetic energy as the slotted mass at 2R.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish shared angular speed from radius-dependent speed and centripetal force.
questions.misconception: Confusing linear speed and angular speed.

explanation.body: The masses share the disc’s angular speed $\omega$ while they rotate with it. Static friction supplies the required centripetal force $mr\omega^2$, which is greatest at $6R$. For identical masses on the same surface, the maximum static friction is the same, so the outermost mass reaches that limit first.

perOption.A: At fixed angular speed, the required centripetal force increases with radius.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass at $6R$ requires the greatest static friction.
perOption.C: All three masses complete the same number of revolutions per unit time while co-rotating.
perOption.D: Kinetic energy scales with the square of linear speed, giving a factor of nine.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The hour hand of a large clock is $2.5\ \mathrm{m}$ long.

What is the average angular speed of this hand?

A $1.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$
B $3.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$
C $1.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$
D $1.0\times10^{-1}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 9: The hour hand of a large clock is 2.5 m long. What is the average angular speed of this hand?

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The only calculation is dividing one revolution in radians by the 12-hour period in seconds.
questions.misconception: Using the minute hand's period.

explanation.body: The hour hand takes $T=12\times60\times60\ \mathrm{s}$ to complete one revolution. Its angular speed is $\omega=2\pi/T\approx1.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses a six-hour period, doubling the angular speed.
perOption.C: Uses the one-hour period of the minute hand.
perOption.D: Implies roughly a one-minute period, treating the hour hand as a seconds hand.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A sphere moves in a horizontal circle with constant angular speed.

What is its linear speed and its centripetal acceleration when the radius of the horizontal circle is halved and angular speed is doubled?

linear speed | centripetal acceleration
A halved | constant
B halved | doubled
C constant | constant
D constant | doubled

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A sphere moves in a horizontal circle with constant angular speed. What is its linear speed and its centripetal acceleration when the radius of the horizontal c

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must apply both changes and account for the square of angular speed in the acceleration.
questions.misconception: Assuming unchanged linear speed means unchanged centripetal acceleration.

explanation.body: The linear speed is $v=r\omega$ and the centripetal acceleration is $a=\omega^2r$. With radius $r/2$ and angular speed $2\omega$, the new linear speed is $(r/2)(2\omega)=v$. The new centripetal acceleration is $(r/2)(2\omega)^2=2a$.

perOption.A: Ignores the doubled angular speed in the speed calculation and misses the doubling of acceleration.
perOption.B: Accounts for the smaller radius alone when calculating the linear speed.
perOption.C: Treats the acceleration as constant because the linear speed stays constant, overlooking the halved radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A pail of water is spun vertically in a circular motion with a radius of $1.3\ \mathrm m$ as shown.

[A dashed vertical circle has a horizontal radius marked $1.3\ \mathrm m$. The water-filled pail is at the bottom, with a rightward velocity arrow labelled $9.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.]

The mass of water is $0.52\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the speed of the pail at the bottom of the circle is $9.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

What is the normal contact force acting on the water at the bottom of the circle?

A $5.1\ \mathrm N$
B $30\ \mathrm N$
C $35\ \mathrm N$
D $40\ \mathrm N$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: A pail of water is spun vertically in a circular motion with a radius of 1.3 m as shown. The mass of water is 0.52 kg and the speed of the pail at the bottom of

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the upward resultant and include the downward weight.
questions.misconception: Equating the normal force with the centripetal resultant.

explanation.body: At the bottom, the inward direction is upward, so $N-mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $N=mg+mv^2/r=0.52(9.3^2/1.3+9.81)=39.7\ \mathrm N\approx40\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Equates the normal force to the weight, giving zero upward acceleration.
perOption.B: Subtracts the weight from the required inward resultant.
perOption.C: Gives the inward resultant alone and omits the downward weight.
perOption.D: Correct. The normal force supplies the inward resultant and balances the weight.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A particle moves at a constant speed in a circular path.

If the radius of the path is doubled while the period of rotation remains the same, what happens to the centripetal acceleration?
questions.stemText: A particle moves at a constant speed in a circular path. If the radius of the path is doubled while the period of rotation remains the same, what happens to the centripetal acceleration? A It increases by a factor of 4. B It is doubled. C It is halved. D It remains the same.

options.label: A
options.text: It increases by a factor of 4.

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Choose the right form of the acceleration formula when the period is fixed.
questions.misconception: Using $a = v^2/r$ while treating $v$ as constant

explanation.body:
$a_c = r\omega^2 = r\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$.

With $T$ unchanged, $a_c \propto r$, so doubling $r$ gives $a_{\text{new}} = 2a_c$.

perOption.A: Treats $a = v^2/r$ as $\propto v^2$ only, forgetting that $r$ also doubles in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $a = v^2/r$ with $v$ held constant, but $v = 2\pi r/T$ doubles.
perOption.D: Ignores the dependence on $r$ at fixed period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, orbits in a circle around Saturn with a radius of 1.22 × $10^{6}$ km. It has an orbital period of 15.9 days.

What is the centripetal acceleration of Titan?
questions.stemText: Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, orbits in a circle around Saturn with a radius of 1.22 × 106 km. It has an orbital period of 15.9 days. What is the centripetal acceleration of Titan? A 4.06 × $10^{-3}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 2.55 × $10^{-2}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 9.19 × $10^{-2}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 1.55 × $10^{3}$ m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must convert the orbital data to SI units and use angular speed in the acceleration formula.
questions.misconception: Omitting a factor of $2\pi$ when converting period to angular speed.

explanation.body: Convert the radius to $1.22\times10^9\ \mathrm{m}$ and the period to $(15.9)(24)(3600)\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $a=r\omega^2$ gives $a=(1.22\times10^9)\left[\frac{2\pi}{(15.9)(24)(3600)}\right]^2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\approx2.55\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Omits one factor of $2\pi$ in the squared angular-speed term.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Arises from leaving the radius in kilometres and converting the period to minutes.
perOption.D: Would require an angular speed much greater than the given orbital period implies.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A record on a turntable rotates at a constant number of revolutions per second.

Which graph best represents the relationship between the linear speed v of a point on the record and its distance r from the centre of the rotation?
questions.stemText: A record on a turntable rotates at a constant number of revolutions per second. Which graph best represents the relationship between the linear speed v of a point on the record and its distance r from the centre of the rotation? A v 0 r 0 B v 0 r 0 C v 0 r 0 D v 0 r 0

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: One direct proportionality determines the shape and intercept of the graph.
questions.misconception: Confusing a common angular speed with a common linear speed.

explanation.body: All points on the record have the same constant angular speed $\omega$. Since $v=r\omega$, linear speed is directly proportional to radius and the graph is a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the common angular speed as a common linear speed.
perOption.C: Shows speed decreasing as the radius increases.
perOption.D: Shows the slope decreasing even though it equals the constant angular speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows an analogue watch.

What is the average angular velocity of the hour hand?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows an analogue watch. What is the average angular velocity of the hour hand? A 2.31 × $10^{-5}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 7.27 × $10^{-5}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 1.45 × $10^{-4}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 1.75 × $10^{-3}$ rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires one revolution in radians and conversion of 12 hours into seconds.
questions.misconception: Using the minute hand’s period

explanation.body: The hour hand turns through $2\pi$ radians in 12 hours. Its average angular velocity has magnitude $\omega=\theta/t=2\pi/(12\times3600)=1.45\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses one revolution as one radian, omitting the factor of 2π.
perOption.B: Uses a 24-hour period for the hour hand.
perOption.C: Correct. It uses one full turn in 12 hours.
perOption.D: Uses the minute hand’s one-hour period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A drone is performing a vertical circular path stunt for its audience on the ground.

Which diagram shows the resultant acceleration a acting on the drone at the instant where its velocity is V and speeding up?
questions.stemText: A drone is performing a vertical circular path stunt for its audience on the ground. Which diagram shows the resultant acceleration a acting on the drone at the instant where its velocity is V and speeding up? A V a B V a C V a D V a

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine inward acceleration with acceleration along the direction of motion.
questions.misconception: Assuming acceleration in circular motion is always entirely centripetal

explanation.body: At the top of the path, the vertical component is the centripetal acceleration and points down toward the centre. The horizontal component points to the right, along the velocity, because the drone is speeding up. The resultant therefore points down and to the right.

perOption.A: Shows only the centripetal component, so the speed is instantaneously constant.
perOption.B: The leftward component is opposite the velocity and would slow the drone down.
perOption.C: Shows only tangential acceleration and omits the inward component needed to turn.
perOption.D: Correct. Both inward and forward components are shown.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A small object of mass m is suspended from a fixed point O by a light, inextensible cord. The object is raised until the cord is horizontal and then released. It moves in an arc of a circle as shown in the figure.

What is the tension in the cord when it passes through its lowest position at point P?
questions.stemText: A small object of mass m is suspended from a fixed point O by a light, inextensible cord. The object is raised until the cord is horizontal and then released. It moves in an arc of a circle as shown in the figure. m O P What is the tension in the cord when it passes through its lowest position at point P? A zero B mg C 2mg D 3mg

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine energy conservation for speed with Newton's second law for circular motion.
questions.misconception: Taking tension at the lowest point to equal the weight

explanation.body: Let $r$ be the cord length. The drop to P converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, so $mgr=\tfrac12 mv^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2gr}$. At P, $T-mg=mv^2/r=2mg$. Hence $T=3mg$.

perOption.A: Assumes the cord has no tension at the bottom of the swing.
perOption.B: Balances the weight and leaves no inward resultant.
perOption.C: Uses the inward resultant force as the tension.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object of mass m is attached to a rigid rod and spun in a uniform vertical circular motion with radius r and a linear velocity of v.

What is the variation of the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the object over one revolution?
questions.stemText: An object of mass m is attached to a rigid rod and spun in a uniform vertical circular motion with radius r and a linear velocity of v. What is the variation of the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the object over one revolution? A zero B 2g C v 2 r D v 2 2 r

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Distinguishes a vector's constant magnitude from its changing direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing acceleration magnitude with its change

explanation.body: The speed $v$ remains constant in uniform circular motion. With fixed radius $r$, the magnitude $a_{\mathrm{c}}=v^2/r$ stays constant, so its variation over a revolution is zero.

perOption.A: Correct. The magnitude stays constant throughout the revolution.
perOption.B: Confuses gravity's effect on the rod force with a change in centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: Gives the constant magnitude itself.
perOption.D: Uses the difference between opposite acceleration vectors when the question asks about changes in magnitude.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A body is moving in a circular path with a radius of 7.70 cm. The time for one orbit is 2.36 s.

What is the centripetal acceleration of the body?
questions.stemText: A body is moving in a circular path with a radius of 7.70 cm. The time for one orbit is 2.36 s. What is the centripetal acceleration of the body? A 0.109 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ B 0.206 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ C 0.368 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ D 0.546 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Straight substitution into a = rω² with ω = 2π/T and a unit conversion.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the cm to m conversion or omitting 2π

explanation.body: The centripetal acceleration is $a=r\omega^2=r(2\pi/T)^2$. With $r=7.70\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m$ and $T=2.36\ \mathrm s$, this gives $a=0.546\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the acceleration by using too small a value for the squared angular speed.
perOption.B: The value is $r\omega$, which is the tangential speed in metres per second.
perOption.C: Underestimates the acceleration given by multiplying the radius by the squared angular speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two objects of masses $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ are fixed on a horizontal circular platform $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from the centre respectively.

When the platform is rotated with uniform circular motion, what is the ratio of the net force on the $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass to the $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass?

A $8:15$
B $5:24$
C $15:8$
D $24:5$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: Two objects of masses 5.0 kg and 8.0 kg are fixed on a horizontal circular platform 2.0 m and 6.0 m from the centre respectively. When the platform is rotated w

appearances.originalFile: grail:9613 DHS 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The shared angular speed cancels in a direct centripetal-force ratio.
questions.misconception: Assuming the masses share a linear speed.

explanation.body: The net force is the centripetal force, $F=mr\omega^2$. The forces on the $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ masses are $(5.0)(2.0)\omega^2=10\omega^2$ and $(8.0)(6.0)\omega^2=48\omega^2$, respectively. Both masses have the same $\omega$, so the ratio is $10:48=5:24$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio obtained by assuming both masses have the same linear speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the inverse-radius dependence for equal linear speeds, although the platform fixes the angular speed.
perOption.D: Reverses the order of the two forces.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A ball of mass 0.10 kg is attached to a string and swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.50 m, as shown. Its speed at the top of the circle is 6.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

What is the tension in the string at this moment?
questions.stemText: A ball of mass 0.10 kg is attached to a string and swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.50 m, as shown. Its speed at the top of the circle is 6.0 m s−1. What is the tension in the string at this moment? A 0.98 N B 6.2 N C 7.2 N D 8.2 N

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single Newton's second law equation at the top of a vertical circle.
questions.misconception: Adding weight to the centripetal force instead of subtracting

explanation.body: At the top, tension and weight both act downwards towards the centre, so $T+W=mv^2/r$. The required resultant is $0.10(6.0)^2/0.50=7.2\ \mathrm{N}$ and the weight is $0.10(9.81)=0.98\ \mathrm{N}$. Hence $T=7.2-0.98=6.22\ \mathrm{N}\approx6.2\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives the ball’s weight alone.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the entire centripetal force and ignores the contribution of weight.
perOption.D: Adds the weight even though it already acts towards the centre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A disc of radius $r$ undergoes uniform circular motion. The speed of point X is $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and its period is 3.2 s. [Diagram: spinning disc; X on the rim at radius $r$, Y on the same radius at $r/2$ from the centre] What are the speed and the period of point Y? (speed / m s$^{-1}$, period / s) A 0.25, 1.6 B 0.25, 3.2 C 0.50, 1.6 D 0.50, 3.2

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A disc of radius r undergoes uniform circular motion. The speed of point X is 1.0 m s−1, and its period is 3.2 s. spinning disc What are the speed and the perio

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of $v = r\omega$ with common angular velocity.
questions.misconception: Thinking points at different radii on a rigid disc have different periods

explanation.body: All points on the rigid disc complete one revolution in the same time, so Y has period $3.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $v=r\omega$ and Y is half as far from the centre as X, $v_Y=0.5v_X=0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Scales the speed with the square of the radius and halves the shared period.
perOption.B: Scales the speed with the square of the radius.
perOption.C: Halves the period along with the speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A stone of mass $m$ is attached to a string. The stone is made to rotate in a vertical circle of radius $r$, as shown. [Diagram: dashed vertical circle of radius r; stone at the top, string vertical down to the centre, velocity v drawn horizontally to the left.] At the point where the stone is vertically above the centre of the circle, the speed of the stone is $v$. Which of the following expressions gives the tension in the string? A $mg - \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ B $\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ C $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} - mg$ D $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} + mg$

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A stone of mass m is attached to a string. The stone is made to rotate in a vertical circle of radius r, as shown. stone of mass m v string r At the point where

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard vertical-circle force balance at the top.
questions.misconception: Treating tension as the only centripetal force or getting the sign of weight wrong

explanation.body: At the top of the circle, both tension and weight point down towards the centre. Their sum is the required centripetal force, so $T+mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $T=mv^2/r-mg$.

perOption.A: This reverses the subtraction needed to isolate the tension.
perOption.B: This attributes the entire centripetal force to tension and omits weight.
perOption.C: Correct. Weight supplies part of the required inward force.
perOption.D: This uses the sign appropriate to the bottom of the circle, where weight points away from the centre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two identical objects rest on a rough, flat, horizontal turntable.

The turntable starts to rotate about its central axis O at an increasing angular velocity.

Initially, both objects are moving in uniform circles.

At a particular angular velocity, one of the objects slides off the turntable.

Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: Two identical objects rest on a rough, flat, horizontal turntable. The turntable starts to rotate about its central axis O at an increasing angular velocity. Initially, both objects are moving in uniform circles. At a particular angular velocity, one of the objects slides off the turntable. Which of the following statements is correct? A The friction experienced by P and Q are always equal. B P experiences larger friction than Q. C Q will start to slide first as it has a larger angular velocity. D Q will start to slide first as it is at a larger radius.

options.label: A
options.text: The friction experienced by P and Q are always equal.

options.label: B
options.text: P experiences larger friction than Q.

options.label: C
options.text: Q will start to slide first as it has a larger angular velocity.

options.label: D
options.text: Q will start to slide first as it is at a larger radius.

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Qualitative use of $F = mr\omega^2$ with friction providing the centripetal force.
questions.misconception: Thinking objects further out have a larger angular velocity

explanation.body: Friction supplies the centripetal force $mr\omega^2$. Before slipping, Q needs more friction because both objects share the same angular velocity and Q is farther from the axis. Q reaches the maximum available static friction first.

perOption.A: Q needs more friction than P before slipping.
perOption.B: P needs less friction because it is closer to the axis.
perOption.C: Q and P have the same angular velocity while they rotate with the turntable.
perOption.D: Correct. Q reaches the friction limit first.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A metal bob is suspended with a light inextensible cord from the ceiling. It is set to whirl in a horizontal circle of radius $r$ with a constant speed such that the cord is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the vertical as shown in the diagram. [Diagram: conical pendulum, cord at angle $\theta$ to the vertical, bob moving in a horizontal circle of radius $r$] Determine the period of rotation for the metal bob. A $\sqrt{4\pi^2 r/g}$ B $\sqrt{4\pi^2 r/(g\sin\theta)}$ C $\sqrt{4\pi^2 r/(g\tan\theta)}$ D $\sqrt{4\pi^2/(gr\tan\theta)}$

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A metal bob is suspended with a light inextensible cord from the ceiling. It is set to whirl in a horizontal circle of radius r with a constant speed such that

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Resolving tension for a conical pendulum and converting angular velocity to period.
questions.misconception: Using the wrong trigonometric ratio when resolving tension

explanation.body: If $F_T$ is the tension and $T$ is the period, the horizontal component satisfies $F_T\sin\theta=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. Vertically, $F_T\cos\theta=mg$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=4\pi^2r/(gT^2)$, so $T=\sqrt{4\pi^2r/(g\tan\theta)}$.

perOption.A: Drops the $\tan\theta$ factor from the force ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the horizontal projection factor and misses the vertical component in the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts $r$ in the denominator, giving the wrong dimensions for a period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A body enters the vertical circular track of radius r shown below with speed v.

If the body falls off the track as shown above, what is a possible value of v?
questions.stemText: A body enters the vertical circular track of radius r shown below with speed v. r v If the body falls off the track as shown above, what is a possible value of v? A gr B 2gr C 4gr D 6gr

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must bound v using energy conservation: enough to rise above the centre but not enough to complete the loop.
questions.misconception: Thinking v = √(gr) at the bottom is the condition for completing the loop

explanation.body: At mid-height the limiting speed is zero, so energy conservation gives $\tfrac12mv^2=mgr$ and a minimum entry speed of $\sqrt{2gr}$. At the top, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force at the contact threshold, so the minimum speed there is $\sqrt{gr}$. For an entry speed just sufficient to maintain contact at the top, $\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mgr=mg(2r)$, giving $v=\sqrt{5gr}$. The body leaves the track between mid-height and the top, so $\sqrt{2gr}<v<\sqrt{5gr}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little entry energy to reach mid-height.
perOption.B: Only reaches mid-height with zero speed.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the minimum entry speed needed to maintain contact throughout the loop.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A conical pendulum consists of a mass of 2.0 kg attached to a light inextensible string of length 1.5 m. The string has a breaking tension of 30 N.

[Diagram: a 2.0 kg bob on a 1.5 m string hanging from a fixed point and moving in a horizontal circle (dashed ellipse) below the point of suspension; a dashed vertical line runs from the suspension point to the centre of the circle.]

What is the maximum speed at which the mass can move in a horizontal circle before the string breaks?

A $3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   B $3.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   C $4.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   D $4.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 8: A conical pendulum consists of a mass of 2.0 kg attached to a light inextensible string of length 1.5 m. The string has a breaking tension of 30 N. 1.5 m 2.0 kg

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must resolve the tension in two directions, use the right radius and eliminate the unknown angle.
questions.misconception: Taking the string length as the radius of the circular path

explanation.body:
Let $\theta$ be the angle the string makes with the vertical, so $r = L\sin\theta$:

$T\cos\theta = mg$ and $T\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{L\sin\theta} \Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{LT}$

Using $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$: $\dfrac{mv^2}{LT} + \left(\dfrac{mg}{T}\right)^2 = 1$

$\dfrac{(2.0)v^2}{(1.5)(30)} = 1 - \left[\dfrac{(2.0)(9.81)}{30}\right]^2 \Rightarrow v = 3.59 \approx 3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Correct. Resolve $T$ vertically and horizontally with $T = 30\ \mathrm{N}$ and $r = L\sin\theta$.
perOption.B: Mixes up the vertical and horizontal components of the tension.
perOption.C: Uses the string length $L$ as the radius of the circle instead of $L\sin\theta$.
perOption.D: Ignores the weight and takes the whole tension as the centripetal force with $r = L$.

questions.stemText:
A car on a horizontal road travels round a corner. The corner is an arc of a circle. When the road is dry, the maximum safe speed is $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

When the road is wet, the maximum frictional force between the surface of the road and the wheels of the car is halved.

What is the maximum safe speed of the car for it to travel round the corner when the road is wet?

A $7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   B $11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   C $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$   D $21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A car on a horizontal road travels round a corner. The corner is an arc of a circle. When the road is dry, the maximum safe speed is 30 m s−1. When the road is

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A simple proportionality argument once friction is identified as the centripetal force.
questions.misconception: Assuming the maximum speed is proportional to the friction force

explanation.body:
Friction on the tyres provides the centripetal force: $f_{\max} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

When the road is wet, $f'_{\max} = \dfrac{f_{\max}}{2} = \dfrac{mv_{wet}^2}{r}$, so $\dfrac{mv^2}{2r} = \dfrac{mv_{wet}^2}{r}$.

$v_{wet} = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{30}{\sqrt{2}} = 21.2 \approx 21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Divides the speed by 4, as if $v^2$ were halved twice.
perOption.B: Divides the speed by $2\sqrt{2}$, which does not follow from $f \propto v^2$.
perOption.C: Halves the speed, treating $f$ as proportional to $v$ rather than $v^2$.
perOption.D: Correct. $v \propto \sqrt{f}$, so $v$ falls by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

questions.stemText: Which of the following statements is not true for a stone attached to a rod and swung in a uniform vertical circular motion? A The kinetic energy of the stone is constant throughout the entire circular motion. B The tension in the rod is lowest when the stone is at the highest point of the circular motion. C The magnitude of resultant force acting on the stone changes depending on the position of the stone in the circle.……………………………………………… D The resultant acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.text: The resultant acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle.

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognising uniform speed is enough to test the statement about resultant force.
questions.misconception: Confusing the rod force with the resultant force

explanation.body: In uniform circular motion, the speed $v$ and radius $r$ stay constant. The resultant force is the centripetal force, so its magnitude $F_c=mv^2/r$ is constant throughout the circle.

perOption.A: Constant speed means constant kinetic energy.
perOption.B: At the top, weight contributes its full magnitude inward, so the rod supplies its smallest signed inward radial force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The acceleration always points towards the centre.

In a particular circular motion, the string makes an angle of 30o with the vertical as shown in the figure below. 3.0 m 5.0 m 30o m central axle What is the period of the mass’s motion about the central axle? A 1.0 s B 3.5 s C 4.8 s D 6.2 s

questions.difficultyReason: Radius includes an offset from the axle and the resolved tension supplies the centripetal force.
questions.misconception: Using the string length as the circle radius

explanation.body:
Vertical: $T\cos30^\circ = mg$ (1). Horizontal: $T\sin30^\circ = mr\omega^2$ (2).

(2)/(1): $\tan30^\circ = r\omega^2/g$, with $r = 3.0+5.0\sin30^\circ = 5.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.B: Uses $r=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ or similar wrong radius.

C: cosine-like with a maximum at 0 and $2\pi$ and a minimum at $\pi$. D: starts low, maximum at $\pi$, falls to low at $2\pi$.]

appearances.originalFile: grail:10482 TJC 2023 H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Choose the right graph shape from $T = mr\omega^2 + mg\cos\theta$.
questions.misconception: Thinking the tension is constant because the speed is constant

explanation.body:
Tangentially: $F - mg\sin\theta = 0$. Radially: $T - mg\cos\theta = mr\omega^2$.

So $T = mr\omega^2 + mg\cos\theta$, which varies with $\cos\theta$.

Tension is largest at the lowest point ($\theta=0$) and smallest at the highest point ($\theta=\pi$), matching graph C.

perOption.A: Constant tension would need no weight component.
perOption.B: Has two cycles per revolution; $\cos\theta$ has one.
perOption.C: Correct. Maximum at $\theta=0$, minimum at $\theta=\pi$.
perOption.D: Minimum at $\theta=0$, which is reversed.

questions.stemText: A turntable consists of a rotating horizontal disc moving at a fixed rotational speed. Which correctly relates P and Q's linear speeds and centripetal forces? questions.difficultyReason: Direct application of $v=r\omega$ and $F=mr\omega^2$ at fixed $\omega$.
questions.misconception: Equating linear speeds of points on a rotating disc

explanation.body:
P and Q are on the same turntable, so they have the same angular velocity $\omega$.

Linear speed $v = r\omega$ is greater for P since $r_1 > r_2$.

Centripetal force $F = mr\omega^2$ is also greater for P since $r_1 > r_2$.

perOption.A: Speeds differ because $v=r\omega$; and the force is greater for P, not Q.
perOption.B: Same angular speed does not mean same linear speed.

perOption.D: Correct. Both $v$ and $F$ increase with $r$ at fixed $\omega$.

questions.stemText: A cart of mass m goes round a vertical loop of radius r before racing over a hill of radius of curvature 2r as shown. Assume resistive forces are negligible. A 0 B mg/2 C mg D 3mg/2

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A cart of mass m goes round a vertical loop of radius r before racing over a hill of radius of curvature 2r as shown in the diagram. P Q If the cart just remain

appearances.originalFile: grail:14595 2024 TJC H2 Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Chains the loop-top condition, energy conservation at equal heights and a hill-top force equation.
questions.misconception: Using $N+mg=mv^2/r$ at the top of the hill

explanation.body:
At P (just in contact, $N\approx0$): $mg = mv^2/r$, so $v^2 = rg$.

P and Q are at the same height, so the kinetic energy (and speed) at Q equals that at P.

At Q: $mg - N = mv^2/(2r)$, so $N = mg - m(rg)/(2r) = mg/2$.

By Newton's third law the cart exerts $mg/2$ on the track.

perOption.A: The cart still needs less than $mg$ of centripetal force at Q, so $N$ is not zero.
perOption.B: Correct. $N = mg - mv^2/2r = mg/2$.
perOption.C: Ignores the centripetal force needed at Q.
perOption.D: Adds instead of subtracts; at the top of a hill, $mg$ exceeds $N$.

[Diagram: vertical wheel with a passenger at the top and at the bottom.]
Force at top / force at bottom: A 1640 N down / 133 N up; B 1640 N up / 133 N down; C 133 N down / 1640 N up; D 133 N up / 1640 N down.

stemImage.alt: Question 10: On a fairground ride, passengers are rotated in a vertical wheel of radius 4.00 m. Passengers complete one revolution in 3.70s. A passenger of mass 77.0 kg is s

questions.difficultyReason: Two free-body diagrams in a vertical circle with consistent sign choices.
questions.misconception: Assumes the same force direction at top and bottom.

explanation.body:
Net force towards the centre is $mr\omega^2$, with $\omega = 2\pi/3.7$.

Top: $F_{top} + mg = mr\omega^2$, so $F_{top} = 77[4(2\pi/3.7)^2 - 9.81] = 133\ \mathrm{N}$ downwards.

perOption.B: Gives the right magnitudes at the wrong positions with wrong directions.
perOption.C: Correct. At the top the wheel pushes down (weight helps); at the bottom it pushes up.
perOption.D: Right magnitudes but directions reversed.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must combine energy conservation, radial dynamics and Newton’s third law.
questions.misconception: The normal force equals the centripetal force.

explanation.body: The loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy, so $mgh=\frac12mv^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2gh}$. At the bottom, $N-mg=mv^2/R$, so $N=mg+2mgh/R=mg(1+2h/R)$. By Newton’s third law, the block exerts a force of this magnitude downward on the track.

perOption.A: Sets the normal force equal to the weight, giving zero radial acceleration.

explanation.body:
At the top of the circle both the weight and the tension act downwards, towards the centre, so the net (centripetal) force is $mg + T$.

perOption.D: Correct. $mv^2/r = T + mg = 5mg$.

A mass $m$, attached to one end of an inextensible string of length 5.0 m, is made to move in a horizontal circle as the central axle is rotated. In a particular circular motion, the string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical as shown.

[Diagram: a vertical central axle with a horizontal arm of length 3.0 m at the top. From the end of the arm hangs a 5.0 m string at $30^\circ$ to the vertical (dashed), with mass $m$ at its lower end, pointing away from the axle.]

What is the period of the mass's motion about the central axle?

A 1.0 s
B 3.5 s
C 4.8 s
D 6.2 s

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The mass at the end of a pendulum is made to move in a horizontal circle of radius $r$ at constant speed. The magnitude of the net force on the mass is $F$.

[Diagram: a conical pendulum; the string hangs from a point above the centre of a dashed horizontal circle of radius r, with the bob on the circle.]

What is the direction of $F$ and the work done by $F$ during half a revolution?

| | direction of F | work done by F |
|---|---|---|
| A | towards centre of circle | zero |
| B | towards centre of circle | $\pi rF$ |
| C | away from centre of circle | zero |
| D | away from centre of circle | $\pi rF$ |

stemImage.alt: Question 8: The mass at the end of a pendulum is made to move in a horizontal circle of radius r at constant speed. The magnitude of the net force on the mass is F. What is

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of centripetal force direction and that a perpendicular force does no work.
questions.misconception: Believing there is an outward (centrifugal) net force, or that a force always does work over a distance

explanation.body:
In uniform circular motion, the net force (the centripetal force) points towards the centre of the circle.

There is no displacement in the direction of the net force, since it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the work done by $F$ is zero.

perOption.A: Correct. Centripetal force is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work.
perOption.B: $\pi rF$ treats the force as acting along the path; it is perpendicular to it.
perOption.C: The net force is centripetal, towards the centre, not outwards.
perOption.D: Wrong direction, and the force does no work since it is perpendicular to the velocity.

questions.stemText:
A stone of weight 3.0 N is fixed, using glue, to one end P of a rigid rod CP as shown in the diagram. The rod is rotated about end C so that the stone moves in a vertical circle of radius 85 cm.

[Diagram: a dashed vertical circle of radius 85 cm centred at C; rod CP with the stone glued at P on the circle, rotating with angular speed $\omega$.]

The angular speed $\omega$ of the rod and stone is gradually increased from zero until the glue snaps when the tension in it is 18 N.

What is the angular speed of the stone?

A $2.4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$  B $7.6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$  C $9.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$  D $58\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying the lowest point as the critical position and converting weight to mass.
questions.misconception: Assuming the critical position in a vertical circle is always the top

explanation.body:
The glue will snap at the lowest position of the vertical circle, where the tension it must supply is greatest.

At the bottom: $T - W = mr\omega^2$

$18 - 3 = \left(\dfrac{3}{9.81}\right)(0.85)\,\omega^2$

$\omega = 7.6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Uses the weight 3.0 N as the mass instead of $m = W/g$.
perOption.B: Correct. Snapping occurs first at the lowest point.
perOption.C: Uses $T + W = mr\omega^2$, the condition at the top, where the glue tension is smallest.
perOption.D: This is $\omega^2$, not $\omega$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The figure below shows a siren disk that has 16 holes near the edge which are equally spaced apart. When the disk is spun in front of a fast-moving jet of air, the holes modulate the air-jet to produce a sound of a particular frequency.

The time it takes for successive holes to move past the air jet is the period of the sound wave.

What is the angular speed of rotation if the frequency of the sound produced is 2200 Hz?
questions.stemText: The figure below shows a siren disk that has 16 holes near the edge which are equally spaced apart. When the disk is spun in front of a fast-moving jet of air, the holes modulate the air-jet to produce a sound of a particular frequency. The time it takes for successive holes to move past the air jet is the period of the sound wave. What is the angular speed of rotation if the frequency of the sound produced is 2200 Hz? A 430 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 860 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 1730 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 3650 rad $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Novel context: must realise one sound period corresponds to 1/16 of a revolution.
questions.misconception: Treating the sound frequency as the rotation frequency

explanation.body:
The period of the sound wave is $T = \frac{1}{f}$, the time for the disc to turn from one hole to the next.

Angle between successive holes: $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{16} = \frac{\pi}{8}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

$\omega = \frac{\theta}{T} = \theta f = \frac{\pi}{8}(2200) = 864\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Uses $\pi/16$ instead of $2\pi/16$ for the angle between holes.
perOption.B: Correct. $\omega = (\pi/8)(2200) \approx 860\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Doubles the correct angle between holes (uses $2\pi/8$).
perOption.D: Does not divide the full-revolution angle correctly among the 16 holes.

questions.stemText:
A stone is placed on a turntable which is rotating with a constant angular velocity.

What changes occur in the linear speed and in the centripetal acceleration of the stone when it is placed at a larger distance from the centre of the turntable?

linear speed | centripetal acceleration
A constant | decrease
B constant | increase
C increase | constant
D increase | increase

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A stone is placed on a turntable which is rotating with a constant angular velocity. What changes occur in the linear speed and in the centripetal acceleration

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Both quantities follow directly from their radius dependence at fixed angular velocity.
questions.misconception: Equating constant angular velocity with constant linear speed.

explanation.body: Since $v=r\omega$ and $\omega$ is constant, the linear speed increases with radius. The centripetal acceleration $a=r\omega^2$ also increases with radius.

perOption.A: Treats linear speed as fixed and then predicts a decrease in centripetal acceleration.
perOption.B: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant linear speed.
perOption.C: Overlooks the radius factor in $a=r\omega^2$.
perOption.D: Correct.
